reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes a beginner-friendly BNB flash-loan arbitrage bot with huge-profit and passive-income claims, while instructing viewers to deploy code, pay fees, and fund the setup with BNB. The speaker reports earning about 0.3 BNB in roughly an hour and gives minimum and recommended funding amounts alongside statements that funds or gas will be returned under stated conditions. Although the speaker says the bot is free and not intended for profit, the video still connects wallet deployment, cryptocurrency funding, and fee payment to the profit claims.

opening.argument: The presentation contains material qualifications that undercut a deceptive guarantee. The speaker says the bot is a hobby offered free and without an intention to profit, and explains that performance is variable: the process may take minutes, an hour, or even two hours. The description likewise makes the return conditional on an opportunity and says that without one, the user is refunded the funds and gas cost. That is uncertainty and limitation language, not an unconditional promise that every viewer will earn money. The reported result is presented as one instance, while the speaker explicitly says it is not instant and tells viewers to take their time.

Sometimes it's just a couple of minutes, but we had cases also where it takes like two. Hours.
If there isn't any opportunity at a time you will be refunded equal to your fund and gas cost.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution treats profit language and transaction steps as if they eliminate the qualifications. They do not. The speaker expressly denies an intention to profit, describes the offering as free, and warns that results are delayed and opportunity-dependent. The cited deployment and fee instructions establish how the demonstration operates; they do not establish a guaranteed return, a required payment to the speaker, or deception. Even the reported result is framed as a personal outcome, not a promise to every viewer.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The qualifications do not neutralize the central inducement. The same presentation says viewers can make huge profits, reports roughly 0.3 BNB, and supplies minimum and recommended funding amounts. Calling the bot free does not make the viewer's required BNB funding and transaction fees risk-free. The refund statement is merely the speaker's claim; the supplied evidence does not independently verify that funds or gas are actually returned.

opening.argument: The video's dominant activity is an operational technology tutorial. It explains how to install and connect a wallet, select a compiler, create a file, paste code, compile the contract, and transact through Remix. The description itself identifies the activity as learning how to flash-loan arbitrage and deploying a smart contract. The screen sequence shows the Remix compiler and deployment interface, followed by a wallet interface, which is consistent with demonstrating a workflow rather than merely making a sales pitch. The speaker also presents a personal test result and explains when the bot was stopped. A tutorial can discuss possible profits without becoming a certification that viewers will receive the same outcome.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution's own quotations describe tutorial mechanics: connecting Remix, pasting code, and paying a transaction fee. Those are evidence of a technical demonstration, not proof that the creator solicits money or guarantees an outcome. The description says the aim is to learn flash-loan arbitrage, and the speaker walks through compilation and operation. A reported test result can illustrate what the demonstrated workflow did on that occasion without converting the entire instructional video into a promise.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not change what the tutorial directs viewers to do. It connects a wallet, deploys copied code, pays fees, funds the bot with BNB, and links those steps to profit. The reported 0.3 BNB result and the recommended 1 BNB starting amount make the instruction financially actionable. The educational format therefore functions as promotion of a profit-producing bot, not neutral programming instruction.

opening.argument: The material describes use of a software tool and a blockchain workflow, but does not show the usual mechanism of a scam solicitation. The speaker says the bot is offered for free, and the described transaction fees are network-operation costs rather than a payment to the speaker. The supplied material shows the user working in MetaMask and Remix, including deployment and a wallet balance, but does not show a request for credentials, a downline, or a payment sent to the presenter. It also describes a conditional process: if no arbitrage opportunity exists, the stated outcome is return of the funds and gas cost. Those details fit an ordinary technical service or tool demonstration, with risk and performance left to the user.

citations.quote: I. Offer this for free and not with any intention to make profit.
Flash loans only costs transaction gas.
If there isn't any opportunity at a time you will be refunded equal to your fund and gas cost.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution infers a scam mechanism from the fact that users must fund their own wallet and pay blockchain fees. But the supplied evidence does not show money being sent to the presenter, a credential request, or recruitment. The wallet and Remix screens depict the user's technical setup, while the speaker says the bot itself is free. A tool that has operating costs and variable results is not automatically a fraudulent product or service.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a direct payment to the presenter is not dispositive. The video still directs viewers to deploy code, pay fees, and supply BNB, while presenting huge profits and a personal profit result. The wallet screen demonstrates that funds are involved, and the speaker recommends a minimum and a larger amount. Calling the bot free does not remove the financial inducement or establish that the promised refund and returns occur.
